slides.title: 2 a.m., 40,000 lines, one lost order
slides.tldr: In a plain-text log you can't isolate one customer's story: every request's lines are mixed together.

blocks.body: It's 2 a.m. and support is on the phone: order 5512 was charged but never created. You open the server log and find 40,000 lines, written by three servers and a worker, all mixed together. Nothing tells you which lines belong to this customer.

blocks.code:
[02:01:13] app.INFO: Checkout started
[02:01:13] app.INFO: Checkout started
[02:01:14] app.INFO: Calling payment gateway
[02:01:14] app.ERROR: Payment failed for user ryan@example.com
[02:01:14] app.INFO: Order saved
[02:01:15] app.ERROR: Something went wrong
[02:01:15] app.INFO: Sending confirmation email

marks.tip: Two different customers' requests, but nothing in the line says which is which.
Which order? Which gateway? How much? None of it is here, and the customer's email leaks into the log.
This line answers no question: what broke, and for whom, is a mystery.

blocks.body: A log that can't tell you one request's whole story isn't information, it's noise.

aside.body: In production you can't attach a debugger or set a breakpoint. Your only eyes are what the system writes down itself, so you have to design what to write, and how, before the incident.

items.meaning: A written record of one thing that happened in the system: when, where, what.
The ability to tell what is going on inside a system by looking from outside. Three pillars: logs, metrics, traces.

check.q: Why is it nearly impossible to find order 5512's events in the log above?
check.a: No line carries an order or request identity, and every request's lines are interleaved, so you can't tell which line belongs to whom.

slides.title: Structured logs: a form, not a letter
slides.tldr: Write each log line as JSON: a fixed message, with the changing facts (order_id, gateway) in their own fields, so you can search and count.

blocks.title: The shipping label
blocks.body: Ship a package at a delivery company's counter and nobody accepts a handwritten note. You fill in a form with boxes: sender, receiver, weight, destination. Because each fact has its own box, "how many packages went to Chicago today?" takes a minute to answer. A structured log works the same way: each line is a JSON record with a fixed message and the changing facts in separate fields (the context).

blocks.caption: The same event, written two ways

columns.title: Plain text
items: Payment failed for order 5512: timeout
You search with grep and regex
Every sentence differs, so you can't count "how many times?"
columns.tip: A sentence written for humans. A machine can't pull the individual facts out of it.

columns.title: Structured (JSON)
items: {"message":"payment.failed","order_id":5512,"reason":"timeout"}
Search order_id = 5512 and every line of that order appears
How often payment.failed happened per hour: one query
columns.tip: Every fact sits in its own field. Log tools (Loki, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch) can filter and aggregate by field.

marks.tip: No variables in the message, so every failure groups under one name. Counting, graphing and alerting become easy.
A field of its own: you can filter directly on order_id later.
Pass the whole exception under the exception key and Monolog writes its class, message, code and file and line. The full stack trace needs `includeStacktraces` turned on in the JSON formatter.

blocks.code:
when@prod:
    monolog:
        handlers:
            main:
                type: stream
                path: php://stderr
                level: info
                formatter: monolog.formatter.json

marks.tip: In a container, write to stderr, not to a file. The platform collects the logs and stores them.
This one line turns every log record into a single line of JSON.

blocks.body: Keep the message fixed; put whatever changes in the context.

items.meaning: Key-value facts attached to a log line: order_id, user_id, gateway.
How serious the line is: debug < info < warning < error < critical.
Decides what shape a log record is written in (plain line or JSON).

items: Never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or whole request bodies. Many people can read logs, and they are kept for a long time.
Use the error level only when someone needs to act. If everything is an error, the real ones get buried.
Don't write an info line for every step of a loop. Log storage is billed by the GB.

check.q: Why log payment.failed with order_id in the context instead of "Payment failed for order 5512" as the message?
check.a: A fixed message lets you count and group the event, and a separate order_id field lets you filter directly without regex.

slides.title: Correlation ID: a tracking number for every request
slides.tldr: Give each request a number at the front door, and let a Monolog processor stamp it on every log line automatically.

blocks.title: The package's tracking number
blocks.body: A delivery company sticks a tracking number on the package the moment you book it. Whether it's scanned at the Dallas hub, on the truck or at the Chicago hub, the same number goes into the ledger. Search that number later and the whole journey appears as one list.

A **correlation ID** is that tracking number for a request. Create it once at the front door, or reuse the one an upstream service already sent. Then a Monolog **processor** (a small piece of code that runs just before each log record is written) stamps the number on every line. Nobody has to type it by hand.

marks.tip: Monolog\Attribute\AsMonologProcessor: with this attribute, MonologBundle registers the class as a processor for every log channel.
If nobody supplied a number, the first call creates a new UUID, so console commands and workers get one too.
Put it in extra and the JSON formatter prints correlation_id on every line. The code that writes logs doesn't change.
In a worker or long-running server, one job's number must not stick to the next job. Symfony calls reset() after each job.
A high priority, so the number is set before security or routing write any log lines.
Putting an unchecked outside value into a log lets someone inject fake log lines (log injection).
The number also goes back in the response, so support can read it off a customer's screenshot.

aside.body: Create the number at the door, stamp it on every log, send it along when you call out.

items.meaning: The number of one request inside one service.
The number of the whole journey. It stays the same across every service, queue and worker.

items: In your Vue app, show the response header's number when an error appears: "Something went wrong, code: 0191…". Finding the logs then takes a minute.
user_id or tenant_id can be stamped on every line the same way, with another processor.

check.q: Why use a processor instead of passing correlation_id by hand in every logger call?
check.a: Someone will forget. A processor stamps every log record automatically, so you write it in one place and it works everywhere.

slides.title: The number crosses queues and services too
slides.tldr: Send the correlation ID in the header of outgoing HTTP calls and in a stamp on queued messages, and pick it up again on the other side.

blocks.body: When the request ends, the work doesn't. A refund goes out from a worker, and the payment happens in another service. If the number doesn't cross those borders, the story breaks halfway. So stick it into the header of every outgoing HTTP call (next slide), and onto every message you put in a queue (in Messenger's terms, a **stamp**).

blocks.caption: One number, three places: every log says 0191-ab

nodes.label: Customer
nodes.tip: Pressed Checkout. They have no number: creating it is the server's job.

nodes.label: Shop API
nodes.tip: The first door. The correlation ID is created here and stamped on all of its log lines.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.tip: A separate service. Its own listener reads the X-Correlation-Id header and reuses the same number.

nodes.label: Queue
nodes.tip: The stamp stays stored with the message, so even if a worker picks it up ten minutes later the number isn't lost.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.tip: Takes a message, first makes the stamp's number the current one, then starts the work.

edges.label: The request arrives; the API creates number 0191-ab
The refund message gets the stamp 0191-ab
The worker reads the stamp and logs under the same number

blocks.caption: Order 5512: filter 40,000 lines by 0191-ab and five remain, in time order

rows.tip: The request arrives and gets the number 0191-ab.
The customer's money is taken. This line comes from another service but carries the same number.
The database gave up waiting for a lock, so no order was created. This is where the story broke.
The API puts a refund job on the queue, and the job carries the stamp.
Four seconds later a different process logs under the same number. The customer was charged and never refunded.

marks.tip: A stamp is extra information attached to a message's envelope. It is serialized with the message and travels through the queue.
Runs at dispatch() time, so the request's number sets off together with the message.
A ReceivedStamp means the message came from a transport, so we are now inside a worker.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        buses:
            messenger.bus.default:
                middleware:
                    - App\Observability\CorrelationIdMiddleware

items: For outgoing HTTP calls the next slide wraps the HTTP client, so the header is added for you and the listener on the other side picks it up.
A worker resets its services after each message. Thanks to `reset()`, the old number doesn't stick to the next one.
A retried message keeps its stamp, so the logs of the first attempt and the later ones match under one number.
Only lines logged after you add the number carry it. Old lines can't be searched this way, so set it up before the incident, not during.

check.q: The API's logs have the number, but the worker's logs don't. Where is the gap?
check.a: Either the number was never attached to the message as a stamp when it was sent, or the worker never read it back and made it current. The middleware does both jobs.

slides.title: Outgoing HTTP calls: stamp the header for free
slides.tldr: Wrap Symfony's HTTP client so every outgoing call carries X-Correlation-Id automatically, instead of trusting each developer to add the header.

blocks.body: Passing the header by hand works until one developer forgets it in one place. That call is where the story breaks: the payment service logs under a new number and nobody can connect the two sides. Do for HTTP what the processor did for logs: add it once, for every call.

marks.tip: No X-Correlation-Id header, so the payment service starts a new number and the trail is cut here.
Replaces the default http_client service: every autowired HttpClientInterface now goes through this class.
Added in one place for every outgoing call. No developer has to remember it.

blocks.body: Anything a machine can stamp must never depend on a developer's memory.

items: This decorates only the default `http_client`. A scoped client (from `scoped_clients`) is a separate service and needs the same decoration.
The header also reaches outside companies. Keep the number random, never something secret like a session ID.
The receiving side is the listener from the correlation-id slide: it validates the header and reuses the number.

check.q: Why decorate the HTTP client instead of adding the header in each call?
check.a: One forgotten call breaks the chain at exactly that point. A decorator adds the header to every call from one place.

slides.title: Traces and spans: where did the time go?
slides.tldr: A trace is one request's whole journey; a span is one step and how long it took, so you see where the delay is at a glance.

blocks.title: Time on the tracking page
blocks.body: A delivery company's tracking page doesn't only list where the package went. It also shows how long it sat at each stop: 2 hours at the Dallas hub, 6 hours on the truck, 19 hours at the Chicago hub. Nobody has to tell you where the delay is.

Distributed tracing gives you exactly this picture. One request's whole journey is a **trace**. Each step of it, a query or an outside call, is a **span**, recorded with its start time, its duration and its parent span. **OpenTelemetry** is the open standard and toolkit that creates spans and ships them to a collector, a small service that gathers them for a viewer. Logs tell you what happened; a trace tells you where the time went.

blocks.caption: POST /checkout: the spans of one trace and their durations

items.label: POST /checkout
items.tip: The root span, the whole request. All the spans below are its children and fit inside it; the remaining ~100ms is PHP's own work.

items.label: SELECT cart
items.tip: Reading the cart from the database. Fast, nothing to chase here.

items.label: Stripe API call
items.tip: Almost 80% of the total time is here. The log shows no error, yet this is the real cause of the slowness.

items.label: INSERT order
items.tip: Writing the order to the database, a normal duration.

items.label: message to queue
items.tip: Putting the email job on the queue. The worker's spans join the same trace.

blocks.code:
OTEL_PHP_AUTOLOAD_ENABLED=true
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=shop-api
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318
OTEL_PROPAGATORS=tracecontext,baggage
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1

marks.tip: With the opentelemetry PHP extension and the auto-symfony package installed, spans for requests, HttpClient calls and so on are created automatically.
tracecontext is the W3C traceparent header. It carries the trace ID and the parent span ID from one service to the next.
Keeps the traces of 10% of requests (sampling). Keeping all of them raises storage cost and overhead. The price: the one request you wanted may be in the 90% dropped.
Opening a span by hand for an important step of your own. Keep the name fixed, like a log message.
If you never call end(), the span is never sent, so it goes in finally.

aside.body: Log: exactly what happened. Metric: how often and how fast. Trace: where the time went.

items.desc: The PHP extension that auto-instrumentation needs
The SDK and the OTLP exporter
Creates spans for Symfony requests automatically

use: One request touches several services, queues or outside APIs.
You need to know which step eats the time in a slow request.
avoid: A small app with one server and one database. Correlation IDs and the Symfony Profiler are enough there.

check.q: Checkout takes 3 seconds, yet the log has no errors. What shows you where the delay is?
check.a: The trace of that request. Putting every span's duration side by side shows which step, which query or outside call, took the most time.

slides.title: The average says fine, the customers say slow
slides.tldr: An average response time hides the few slow requests, so measure real experience with percentiles (p90, p99) and metrics collected continuously.

blocks.title: The doctor's vital signs
blocks.body: A nurse measures a patient's temperature, pulse and blood pressure on a schedule and writes them on a chart. You tell whether the patient is doing well from the trend in the numbers, not from the look on their face. A metric is your app's chart: a number measured every minute, piling up over time.

blocks.caption: Response times for the same 100 customers: average vs percentiles

items.label: Average
items.tip: Add everything up and divide. A few very slow requests drown in the average, so it looks great.

items.label: p50
items.tip: The middle customer: half of your customers got an answer faster than this.

items.label: p90
items.tip: 90 of 100 customers got an answer within this time. The other 10 waited longer.

items.label: p99
items.tip: One customer in 100 sat there for 2.4 seconds. They may well be your biggest spender, because big carts make the heaviest pages.

blocks.body: You can't measure experience with an average. Look at p90 and p99, your slowest customers.

aside.title: Monday's complaints
aside.body: Ethan's dashboard showed a green 120ms average. Yet support got "checkout hangs" complaints every day. Once he looked at p99, it turned out customers with big carts were waiting 2 to 3 seconds and many gave up. The average never mentioned them.

items.meaning: p99 is the time within which 99 out of 100 customers got their answer: everyone except the slowest 1%.
A number measured regularly over time: request count, errors, response time.

check.q: The average response time is 120ms, yet p99 is 2.4 seconds. What does that mean?
check.a: Most customers get fast answers, but about 1 in 100 has a much slower experience. The average hid it.

slides.title: Three kinds of metric: counter, gauge, histogram
slides.tldr: A counter only goes up (how many), a gauge moves up and down (how much now), a histogram drops values into buckets (how many took how long). Percentiles come from histograms.

blocks.title: A train conductor's three tallies
blocks.body: The conductor's ticket counter only goes up: how many tickets sold today (a counter). The number of passengers on the train right now rises and falls (a gauge). And how long each passenger took to reach their stop is sorted into bins like "within 10 minutes, within 20 minutes" and counted (a histogram).

cells: Only goes up; resets to zero on restart
rows.tip: For running totals. The useful figure (how many per second) comes from rate(), not from the raw number.
The state right now: how many messages are waiting in the queue, how many connections are open.
Counts which bucket each value fell into. It gives you p50, p90 and p99, and you can combine the values of many servers.

blocks.title: Rules for labels
items: Never label by user_id, order_id or a full URL (/orders/5512): every distinct value starts a new time series (its own line on the graph). 100,000 users × 20 routes is 2 million lines.
Labels should come from a short, bounded list: method, route name, status.
No personal data or tokens in labels.

blocks.body: Keep label values bounded. Make an ID a label and the metrics system itself falls over.

aside.body: Counter: how many. Gauge: how much right now. Histogram: how fast.

items: Reading a counter's raw value: it restarts from zero when the server restarts. Always use rate().
Wrong histogram buckets give wrong percentiles. Put buckets around your SLO threshold (say 0.5 seconds).

items.meaning: How many distinct time series a metric's label combinations produce. The more there are, the more it costs.

check.q: Why is a route name fine as a metric label but user_id is not?
check.a: There are only a few routes, but user_id has millions of values. Each distinct value is a separate time series, so user_id would blow up the metrics system's memory and cost.

slides.title: What to measure: RED and USE
slides.tldr: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services, USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for machines. Measure these six and you catch most problems.

blocks.title: The restaurant's customers and its kitchen
blocks.body: You can judge a restaurant from two sides. From the customer's side: how many orders per hour, how many orders came out wrong, how many minutes the food took (RED). From the kitchen's side: what share of the time the stove is on, how long the order line is, which equipment is broken (USE).

blocks.caption: RED through the service's eyes, USE through the machine's eyes

columns.title: RED: for a service (API)
items: Rate: requests per second
Errors: the share that fail (5xx)
Duration: how long it takes (p50, p99)
columns.tip: Measures what the user feels. It tells you what is broken.

columns.title: USE: for a machine (CPU, DB, queue)
items: Utilization: the share of time it is busy
Saturation: how much work is waiting in line
Errors: how often the machine failed
columns.tip: Measures the machine's health. It tells you why it is broken.

blocks.code:
# Rate: requests per second
sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total[5m]))

# Errors: the share of 5xx
sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total[5m]))

# Duration: p99
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le) (rate(shop_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

# Saturation (USE): messages waiting in the async queue right now
max(shop_queue_depth{queue="async"})

marks.tip: rate() turns a counter into "how many per second"; [5m] means the trend over the last 5 minutes.
A ratio, not a count: 10 failures in 100 requests is dangerous, in a million it is not.
Turns the bucket counts into one p99 number. le means "less than or equal": the upper edge of each bucket.
A gauge, set from Messenger's queue (the next slide shows how). A number that keeps climbing means work is arriving faster than it is handled.

blocks.body: Watch RED on services and USE on machines; saturation shows up first.

items: Build the RED dashboard the same way for every service and for each important endpoint (checkout, login).
Queue depth (saturation) is often the first hint of trouble: the CPU is calm, but work is piling up.

items.meaning: The query language of Prometheus, the database that stores metrics. Each query asks for a number or a graph.
Whether more work is arriving than the machine can handle and is queuing up. A pile-up means delays are coming.

check.q: The API's error rate is fine, but 10,000 messages sit in the queue. Which measure would have caught it?
check.a: USE's saturation, meaning queue depth. The RED numbers look good because the API is answering; the piled-up work is stuck behind it.

slides.title: Adding metrics to Symfony
slides.tldr: A listener bumps a counter and a histogram on every request, and a /metrics endpoint shows them to Prometheus. Label by route name, not URL.

blocks.body: The `promphp/prometheus_client_php` package creates counters and histograms. Prometheus, a database for metrics, visits your `/metrics` page every 15 seconds and stores the numbers. A PHP-FPM request is a short-lived process, so the numbers must live outside it. In `config/services.yaml` point the registry at Redis: `Prometheus\Storage\Redis: {arguments: [{host: '%env(REDIS_HOST)%'}]}` and `Prometheus\CollectorRegistry: {arguments: ['@Prometheus\Storage\Redis']}`.

marks.tip: _route is the route's name (order_show), not the URL. Names are bounded, URLs are not; this is what saves your cardinality.
Status is a label too, so you can compute the share of 5xx.
Put a bucket boundary (0.5 seconds) near your SLO. Then "what percent finished within 0.5 seconds" comes straight out.
Keep this page open only on the internal network (firewall or an nginx allow rule), never on the internet.
A gauge is set, not incremented. Reading the queue at every scrape (every 15 seconds) keeps the number fresh without a separate job.

items: Measure business metrics too: orders_placed_total, payments_failed_total (one inc() in the order handler). Technical metrics can look fine while orders are at zero.
Redis storage gives one shared set of numbers but costs a network call per write. APCu is faster, but each server then keeps (and is scraped for) its own numbers.
Without shared storage, each short-lived request starts from zero and every scrape shows almost nothing.

check.q: What happens if you label by the full URL instead of the route name?
check.a: /orders/1, /orders/2 and so on each become a separate time series. The count explodes, the metrics system's memory and cost grow, and the dashboard becomes unreadable.

slides.title: SLI and SLO: exactly how good is "good"?
slides.tldr: An SLI is a measured ratio (good requests / all requests); an SLO is its target (say 99.9% over 30 days). 100% is never the target.

blocks.title: The class attendance rule
blocks.body: A course rule says you can take the final exam if you attended at least 75% of classes. Classes attended / total classes is a ratio: that's the SLI. The 75% is the target: that's the SLO. And the 25% you are allowed to miss is the error budget.

blocks.title: Three terms
items: SLI: good events / all events. For example: checkout requests answered within 500ms without a 5xx / all checkout requests.
SLO: the target for that ratio over a time window. For example: 99.9% over 30 days.
SLA: a contract with the customer, with penalties if broken. Set looser than the SLO so you get a warning before you break it.

blocks.caption: How much failure fits inside the SLO over 30 days

rows.tip: Can be enough for an internal tool or a low-priority service.
A common target for an ordinary web app.
For critical paths like checkout or payment. Every extra 9 multiplies the cost.
There is no time for a human to handle an incident; everything must be automatic, which makes it very expensive.

blocks.body: An SLO is never 100%. It sits between what customers will feel and what you can afford.

items: Pick SLIs from the customer's side: not "server up" but "checkout succeeded within 500ms". CPU usage is not an SLI.
Give critical paths (login, checkout) a different SLO from low-priority ones (reports).

items.meaning: Always measured over "the last 30 days", not over a calendar month.

aside.body: SLI = measured. SLO = target. SLA = contract.

check.q: A team says "our target is 100% uptime". Why is that a bad SLO?
check.a: 100% is impossible, and chasing it makes cost explode. It also leaves no room for changes or deploys, since every change carries some risk.

slides.title: Error budget: how much risk can we take?
slides.tldr: The failure your SLO tolerates is your budget. While budget remains, ship features fast; when it runs low, focus on stability. Numbers decide, not arguments.

blocks.title: The monthly paid-time-off ledger
blocks.body: If you get 2 days of paid time off a month, you can spend them as you like: travel, try something new. Once they're gone, no more; you stay at work. An error budget is that ledger: as long as some room for failure remains, you can ship new features quickly.

blocks.caption: The team's rules by how much budget is left (99.9% SLO, 30 days, 43-minute budget)

columns.title: More than 50% left
items: Deploy features fast, several times if needed
Experimental changes and risky migrations are fine
columns.tip: Plenty of budget means the system is running better than the SLO. There is room to take risks.

columns.title: 10-50% left
items: Risky changes in small steps
Find what is spending the budget and fix it
columns.tip: The budget is shrinking. Time for more caution and closer watching.

columns.title: Used up
items: No new features, only stability work
Until the budget recovers, or the cause is fixed
columns.tip: This rule is written down in advance, with the team's and managers' agreement, so nobody argues during a crisis.

blocks.file: PromQL: burn-rate alert (99.9% SLO over 30 days)
blocks.code:
# SLI: checkout requests that did not fail with a 5xx
# Over the last hour, is failure eating the budget 14.4x faster than allowed?
(
  sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total{route="checkout",status=~"5.."}[1h]))
  / sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total{route="checkout"}[1h]))
) > (14.4 * 0.001)

marks.tip: 0.001 = 1 - 0.999, the allowed failure rate. At 14.4 times that rate one hour burns 2% of the budget, and all 30 days of it are gone in about 2 days.

blocks.body: Budget left: take risks. Budget gone: stabilize. Numbers decide, not moods.

aside.body: Developers say "we need more features", operations says "we need more stability", and the argument turns into a fight of opinions. An error budget gives both sides one shared number.

items: Look at who ate the budget: one big outage, or small daily failures? The cures differ.
Two tiers of burn-rate alert: fast burn (14.4x, 1 hour) pages someone, slow burn (6x, 6 hours) files a ticket.
Needs enough traffic: at 100 requests a day one failure is 1%, so the ratio jumps around and an SLO means little.

check.q: This month's error budget is gone, but the manager wants to ship a big feature. What should happen?
check.a: Follow the rule written in advance: pause new features and do stability work. If you must make an exception, do it consciously, with agreement, and knowing the risk.

slides.title: The alarm that rings every day, and the day of the real fire
slides.tldr: When an alert fires daily and there is nothing to do, the team learns to ignore it, and one day the real alert gets buried too.

blocks.title: The building's fire alarm
blocks.body: An office fire alarm goes off by mistake every day, sometimes from toaster smoke, sometimes from a drill. After a few weeks nobody walks outside anymore. Then one day there really is a fire, the alarm rings, and everyone thinks "the toaster again". That is alert fatigue.

blocks.caption: Alerts the on-call engineer received last week

items.label: CPU > 70%
items.tip: No customer is hurt and there is nothing to do. It only wakes someone up.

items.label: Disk > 60%
items.tip: It grows slowly. A ticket in the morning would do; it is no reason to wake anyone at night.

items.label: A single 500 error
items.tip: One or two failed requests are normal, so alerting on each one is pointless.

items.label: Worker restart
items.tip: It heals itself and no customer notices.

items.label: Checkout errors > 5%
items.tip: The only real alert: customers can't buy. But among 240 others, everyone took this one for "just another".

blocks.body: An alert that wakes you with nothing to do isn't an alert, it's noise pollution.

aside.title: Failed checkout, 20 minutes late
aside.body: At 2 a.m. checkout started failing. The on-call engineer saw the alert on their phone, thought "the CPU one again", snoozed it and went back to sleep. They learned the truth 20 minutes later from a call from support. By then many orders were lost.
An alert exists to say "a human needs to do something right now". Everything else belongs on a dashboard or in a ticket, not in something that wakes people up.

check.q: Why is it harmful to send an alert for every one or two failed requests?
check.a: Some requests will always fail. The alert fires too often, people learn to ignore it, and the alert for a real crisis gets buried too.

slides.title: Alive or ready: liveness and readiness
slides.tldr: Liveness asks "are you stuck, do you need a restart?", readiness asks "can you take work right now?". Never check the database in liveness.

blocks.title: A bus and taking passengers
blocks.body: Whether the bus engine is running is one question (liveness): if it has died, a mechanic comes and restarts it. Whether the door is open, the driver is in place and the bus is ready to take passengers is a different question (readiness): if it isn't, passengers board another bus, but this one isn't broken.

blocks.caption: The two probes: what they check, what happens on failure

rows.tip: Two different questions, so two different endpoints.

cells: The load balancer stops sending traffic
rows.tip: When readiness fails the process doesn't die; it just gets no traffic for a while. When it recovers, traffic returns.

cells: Essential dependencies other than itself (DB, cache)
rows.tip: Shallow means light on the inside; deep also touches outside dependencies.
Get this wrong and the disaster grows; see the example on the right.

blocks.caption: The restart storm of a liveness probe that checks the database, and the way out

steps.title: 1. The DB gets slow
steps.body: Queries take 3 seconds; the probe's own query waits behind them
steps.tip: Only slowness, not a crash. The database is still working.

steps.title: 2. Liveness fails
steps.body: On every server the probe times out 3 times in a row
steps.tip: The probe blames the app for something that is not the app's fault.

steps.title: 3. All restart at once
steps.body: The platform kills all 10 servers together
steps.tip: For a while nobody is left to serve customers.

steps.title: 4. The stampede
steps.body: Fresh servers open connections and warm caches all at once
steps.tip: The slow database now gets its heaviest load, from every server together.

steps.title: 5. Worse, and again
steps.body: The probe fails again and it is back to step 2
steps.tip: A loop that only ends when somebody turns the probe off.

steps.title: 6. The way out
steps.body: Liveness answers only for itself; a failing readiness just holds traffic back
steps.tip: No process dies, nothing stampedes, and traffic returns as soon as the database does.

blocks.body: Liveness speaks only for itself. When the database is down, restarting every server helps nobody.

aside.title: Slow database, then everything restarts
aside.body: One team's liveness probe touched the database. One day the database got slow, the probe timed out, and the platform restarted every server at once. The fresh servers then all hammered the database together and made it worse.

items.meaning: A small check the platform runs every few seconds against your app: it calls a URL and sees whether it answers well.
The traffic cop in front of your servers. It decides which server gets each request.
For slow-starting apps: it holds the other probes off until the app has started.
Shallow: it only answers for itself. Deep: it also touches dependencies like the DB and cache.

use: In readiness, include only the dependency without which the app can do no work at all.
avoid: Optional or third-party services in readiness: their outage would make all your servers look "sick".

check.q: The database is down. What happens if the liveness probe checks the database?
check.a: The probe fails and every server keeps restarting, yet restarting doesn't fix the database. You only add damage and chaos.

slides.title: Two health endpoints in Symfony
slides.tldr: `/health/live` always returns 200 (it only proves the app is alive), `/health/ready` checks the essential dependencies and returns 503 on failure. Error details go to the log, not the response.

marks.tip: No dependencies: if PHP can answer, it is "alive". The restart decision rests on this alone.
Just "SELECT 1": does the DB connection work? Not a heavy query; probes run every few seconds.
Error details go to the log. Outsiders can't learn stack traces or host names from the health page.
503 means "not now"; the load balancer steers traffic away from this server instead of restarting it.

blocks.code:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health/live, port: 80}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 30
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health/live, port: 80}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health/ready, port: 80}
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 2

marks.tip: Gives a slow-starting app 2.5 minutes (5 seconds x 30) before liveness is allowed to kill it.
Restart only after 3 failures in a row; one slow answer doesn't mean it's dead.
Two failures and traffic stops. timeoutSeconds 2 keeps the probe from hanging on a slow DB.

items: Mark the health pages PUBLIC_ACCESS in the firewall (access_control), so probes need no login. But don't put internal details in the response.
During a deploy, no traffic goes to new code until it is ready. That is the foundation of zero-downtime deploys.
Graceful shutdown: when stopping, fail readiness first, then let in-flight requests finish.
If the shared database is down, every server fails readiness and users get errors. That is honest: no restart would fix it.

check.q: Why does readiness keep a failed dependency's full error message in the log instead of the response?
check.a: Health pages are often open to everyone. A full message with host names, versions or a stack trace would tell an attacker about your internals. So the details stay in the log.

slides.title: A good alert: page on symptoms, not causes
slides.tldr: Page on signs of user harm (errors, slowness, SLO burn), not on causes (CPU, disk). Every alert must be urgent, actionable and come with a runbook.

blocks.title: Smoke in the house vs a warm kitchen
blocks.body: When smoke rises in the house (a symptom), you wake everyone, because harm is coming whatever the cause. But waking someone at 2 a.m. to say "the kitchen is at 95°F" (a cause) is pointless: when cooking is going on, the heat will rise. So wake people for the symptom and hunt for the cause afterwards.

blocks.caption: What to send for which situation

rows.tip: A symptom, urgent, and there is something to do. A true page-worthy alert.

cells: Error budget burning slowly over 6 hours
rows.tip: Not urgent right now, but it grows if ignored; a ticket is enough.
Cause-based, and 15 weeks from full (30% left at 2% a week). A predictive alert, "full in 4 days at this rate", would page only when it matters.
It heals itself; no human action is needed.

blocks.title: Three tests for every alert
items: Urgent: is harm happening or about to? If not, make it a ticket.
Actionable: can a person woken up do something? If not, it isn't an alert.
Runbook: does the alert link to a page saying what to look at and what to do?

blocks.body: Page on symptoms, open tickets for causes, and attach a runbook to every page.

items.meaning: To wake a person with a phone alert, whatever the hour.
A promise about service quality, such as "99.9% of checkouts succeed".
How much failure the SLO allows. Burning it fast means the promise is at risk.
A one-page guide for the person woken: what the alert means and what to do.

items: Review alerts once a month: how often each fired, and how often someone did something. Delete or demote to a ticket any alert nobody acted on.
Add a wait like `for: 5m`: alert on a sustained problem, not a momentary spike.

check.q: Why is paging on CPU at 90% wrong, and what should you page on instead?
check.a: CPU is a cause, not customer harm: everything can run fine at 90% CPU. Page on customer-facing symptoms instead: error rate, latency or SLO burn.

slides.title: A bad alert, a good alert, and the runbook
slides.tldr: Cause-based alerts with no wait ruin sleep. A symptom-based rule with `for`, a severity and a runbook link is the one that works.

marks.tip: A cause, not a symptom. And it doesn't say which server or what to do.
No wait (for): a 1-second spike pages someone, and there is no runbook.

blocks.code:
- alert: CheckoutErrorsHigh
  expr: |
    sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total{route="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total{route="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.05
      and sum(rate(shop_http_requests_total{route="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.2
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page
    team: payments
  annotations:
    summary: 'More than 5% of checkout requests have failed for 5 minutes'
    runbook_url: 'https://wiki.shop.example/runbooks/checkout-errors'

marks.tip: A ratio, so a busy hour and a quiet hour are judged by the same yardstick.
A floor of 12 requests a minute. At 3 a.m. with 4 requests, one failure is already 25%, and nobody should be woken for that.
No alert unless it lasts 5 minutes; momentary spikes are ignored.
Who gets the alert is in the labels. An alert with no owner is handled by nobody.
The runbook link lives inside the alert, so a sleepy brain at 2 a.m. doesn't have to hunt for it.

blocks.caption: The shape of a runbook (one page, readable at 2 a.m.)

steps.title: 1. What this is
steps.body: What the alert means and how customers are hurt
steps.tip: One or two sentences, written to be understood half asleep.

steps.title: 2. Look first
steps.tip: Give direct links, not a list of names.

steps.title: 3. Likely causes
steps.body: A list from past incidents, most likely first
steps.tip: Check recent deploys first; most incidents follow a change.

steps.title: 4. Stop the bleeding
steps.body: Roll back, switch a feature flag off, scale up: stop the symptom first
steps.tip: Finding the cause comes later. Stop the harm first.

steps.title: 5. Who to call
steps.body: The next level's name and phone number
steps.tip: If you can't handle it, call them without wasting time.

items: A runbook gets written and never updated. After every incident, fix any wrong or incomplete step.
Twenty-five alerts for one incident: in Alertmanager, `group_by: [alertname, team]` bundles them into one page.
Nobody knows whose job it is; write the owning team on every alert.

aside.body: Symptom, wait (for), owner, runbook: without all four it's not an alert.

items.label: Handling the incident after the alert

check.q: What does `for: 5m` buy you in an alert rule, and what is its risk?
check.a: A momentary spike no longer fires the alert for nothing. The risk: you hear about a real problem 5 minutes late. So pick the value by looking at the kind of harm and your SLO, so both sides balance.

slides.title: 3 a.m.: everyone's hands in the same pot
slides.tldr: In an outage the biggest danger is often not the root problem but the chaos: five people change production at once and nobody knows what changed.

blocks.title: A fire in the neighborhood
blocks.body: When a fire breaks out in the neighborhood, everyone runs with a bucket. Someone throws water the wrong way, someone blocks the door, and nobody knows where it started. The fire service has a leader, split duties, and one first rule: stop the fire spreading. Finding the cause comes later.

blocks.caption: The same outage, handled two ways

columns.title: Chaotic
items: Five people log into the server and make changes at once
Nobody knows who changed what
A manager asks "what's happening?" every 5 minutes
Customers wait while people hunt for the cause
columns.tip: Everyone means well, but without coordination both time and damage grow.

columns.title: Organized
items: One coordinator, everyone else on their own tasks
Every change is written down in one place
One person updates everyone at fixed intervals
Stop the harm first, find the cause later
columns.tip: With roles and rules decided in advance, work goes on even in a sleepy head.

blocks.body: In an outage, stop the harm first; find the cause later, with a calm head.

aside.title: Two changes canceling each other
aside.body: At 3 a.m. checkout broke. One person rolled back while, at the very same moment, another deployed a hotfix. The two changes canceled each other out and the app got worse. Neither knew what the other was doing.
During an incident minds are under pressure, sleep is short and panic is high. So for good decisions you have to settle rules and roles beforehand.

check.q: What goes wrong when five people change production at once during an incident?
check.a: Nobody knows who changed what, changes can cancel each other out, and you can't tell which one worked. You need one coordinator and one place that lists the changes.

slides.title: Triage: measure the harm first, then decide how urgent
slides.tldr: Don't rush off on hearing about a problem. First ask who is hurt, how badly and for how long; then set a severity, which decides how many people respond and how fast.

blocks.title: The hospital emergency room
blocks.body: When patients arrive at the emergency room, the nurse first checks who is in the worst shape: bleeding before a cold. Treat everyone at the same speed and the one who needs it most dies. Triage means putting limited people and time where they matter most.

blocks.title: The questions of the first five minutes
items: Who is hurt? All customers, some regions, or only the internal team?
How badly? Completely down, slow, or just some features not working?
Since when? What changed right before (deploy, config, traffic)?
Is money or data at risk?

blocks.caption: Severity: how big the incident is, what the response is

cells: Checkout or payment down for everyone, data at risk
Everyone now, a coordinator, update every 30 minutes
rows.tip: Direct harm to money or data. Drop everything else for this.

cells: A major feature broken or very slow, a workaround exists
rows.tip: Customers are hurting, but some paths still work.

cells: A minor feature or a small number of users
rows.tip: It can be fixed in the morning without waking anyone at night.

blocks.body: Measure before you run: who is hurt, how badly, since when.

items: When in doubt, rate the severity higher. You can lower it later, but raising it late costs you.
Write down severity definitions beforehand. At 3 a.m. there is no time to argue "is this a SEV1?".

items.meaning: Measuring the harm and setting priorities so limited people go to the most urgent work.
How many users, or how much of the system, the problem has spread to.

check.q: At 3 a.m. two alerts arrive: "report page slow" and "checkout failing at 20%". Which comes first?
check.a: Checkout: direct money loss, so SEV1 or SEV2. A slow report page is SEV3 and can wait until morning. Setting that order is exactly triage's job.

slides.title: Stop it first, find the cause later
slides.tldr: Mitigation (rollback, feature flag off, scale, failover) stops the harm fast. Hunt for the root cause only when customers are no longer being hurt.

blocks.title: A burst pipe and a flooded house
blocks.body: A pipe has burst and water is spreading through the house. First shut the main valve: the water stops. Then, calmly, find which pipe cracked and why. Hunt for the cause without closing the valve and the whole house floods. Rollback and feature flags are your main valve.

blocks.caption: Five steps you loop through during an incident

steps.title: 1. Read the symptoms
steps.tip: Look at numbers, not guesses: error rate, latency and how many jobs are waiting in the queue.

steps.title: 2. What changed?
steps.body: Deploys, config, traffic just before the start
steps.tip: Behind most outages sits a recent change. It is the likeliest guess.

steps.title: 3. Form a hypothesis
steps.tip: Change many things at once and you can't tell which one worked.

steps.title: 4. Stop it
steps.tip: Safest first: rollback > flag > scale > hotfix.

steps.title: 5. Verify
steps.tip: Don't declare the incident over until you have seen proof that the harm stopped.

blocks.file: terminal: commands for the first few minutes
blocks.code:
# when did it start? what was deployed just before?
kubectl rollout history deployment/shop-api

# when in doubt, go back first and look for the cause later
kubectl rollout undo deployment/shop-api

# is the queue piling up?
php bin/console messenger:stats

# the whole story of one failed request, via its correlation id
kubectl logs deploy/shop-api --since=15m | grep 0191-ab

marks.tip: The list of revisions and when each happened. Compare it with the start time.
Going back to the previous revision. Rolling back code is safe, but a database change does not roll back with it: see the next slide.
With the correlation id built in logging-tracing, one customer's incident comes up in one list.

blocks.body: Stop the harm first, find the cause after, and change one thing at a time.

items: Assuming rollback undoes the database too. It only swaps the code; the next slide shows what breaks and the two-step fix.
Use a feature flag alongside the deploy for rollback: if the new feature sits behind a flag, turning it off is one click.
Logging into a server and editing code directly (a hot patch): in the chaos nobody knows what changed where. Every change goes through the pipeline.

items.meaning: Putting the previous version of the code back, like undoing the last deploy.
A switch in config that turns one feature on or off without a deploy.
Sending traffic to a standby copy (another server or database) when the main one is down.
A quick new code change made in a hurry. The riskiest fix, because it is barely tested.

check.q: A new deploy went out 10 minutes before checkout broke. Roll back first or find the cause first, and why?
check.a: Roll back. A recent change is the likeliest cause, and going back is fast and safe. Only once the harm stops can you look for the cause calmly.

slides.title: When rollback isn't enough: the database moved on
slides.tldr: Rollback swaps the code, not the data. If the deploy also renamed a column, the old code breaks on the new schema, so change the schema in two safe steps.

blocks.body: Rollback puts the old code back, but the database stays exactly as the deploy left it. Say the 13:45 deploy renamed the `phone` column to `mobile`. You roll back, and the old code asks for `phone`, which no longer exists. Every query on customers fails, and the rollback made things worse.

marks.tip: One step: the old column is gone the moment this runs, so the old code can never run again.
The old phone column stays, so after a rollback the old code still finds what it needs.
Only now is the old column dropped, after the new code has run safely for days.

blocks.body: The price: two deploys instead of one, and for a while the data lives in two columns, so the new code must write both. It is worth it on any live app. For a brand-new table nobody reads yet, one step is fine.
Rollback undoes code, not data: change the database in two steps, never one.

use: A live app with real traffic
Any column rename, drop or type change
avoid: A brand-new table that no running code reads yet

check.q: A deploy renamed a column in one step and checkout broke. Why doesn't rolling the code back fix it?
check.a: The old code still asks for the old column, which the migration already removed, so it fails too. Add the new column first and drop the old one in a later deploy.

slides.title: Roles and communication: who does what, who tells whom
slides.tldr: One Incident Commander coordinates (and doesn't touch the keyboard), one person fixes, one keeps everyone informed, and one writes the timeline.

blocks.title: The wedding-feast manager
blocks.body: At a wedding feast the manager doesn't cook. They watch who is doing what, where more hands are needed, and what the guests are told. The cooks cook, and someone else keeps the guests informed. Without that split everyone ends up cooking, and the guests wait with no news.

blocks.caption: Four roles: what they do and what they don't

rows.tip: The one who sees the whole picture. Pick up a task and you lose the picture, so they stay off the keyboard.
The one on the keyboard. When many people want something, they go through the IC.
Managers, support and the status page: so nobody keeps pinging the technical team.

cells: The timeline: who did what, when
rows.tip: The raw material of the later postmortem. A timeline written during the incident beats memory.

blocks.file: status update: the same template every 30 minutes
blocks.code:
[14:20] Update #2 — SEV1, checkout failing

Impact:      about 20% of customers can't place orders (since 13:50)
What we know: payment calls have timed out since the 13:45 deploy
What we're doing: rolling that deploy back; result expected by 14:30
What we don't know: why it timed out; we'll investigate after the rollback

Next update: 14:50 (sooner if anything changes)

marks.tip: In numbers: how many, since when. Not "some issues".
Writing "what we don't know" is honesty: passing a guess off as fact costs trust later.
Name the time of the next update and nobody keeps asking.

blocks.body: Whoever sees the picture doesn't pick up tools; whoever picks up tools doesn't see the picture.

items: On a small team one person can hold several roles, but the IC and Ops are never the same person.
Keep a single incident channel (a chat room or a call) and write every decision and change there. No side conversations.
On the customer-facing status page, write honestly: what is broken, when you expect it back, when the next update is.

aside.title: The manager's calls for lack of updates
aside.body: In one outage nobody told the outside world anything for 40 minutes. The manager, support and a partner each phoned a developer directly, and the real work stopped. A regular update would have prevented those calls.

check.q: What does the Incident Commander lose by grabbing the keyboard and debugging?
check.a: The overall picture. Nobody is then watching who is doing what, what has changed, or who needs to be called. That is why the coordinator stays hands-off.

slides.title: Learning, not blaming: the blameless postmortem
slides.tldr: Ask "who made the mistake?" and people hide mistakes. Ask "why did the system let it happen?" and mistakes get fixed. So write postmortems blameless, with an action list.

blocks.title: A plane crash investigation
blocks.body: After a plane crash, the investigators open the black box. The aim isn't to punish the pilot but to learn: what happened, and why the system let one mistake grow into a disaster. That is why flying gets safer year after year. Pilots admit their mistakes because they know the result will be improvement.

blocks.caption: Two kinds of question, two kinds of outcome

columns.title: Hunting for blame
items: "Who made the mistake?"
Result: people hide mistakes and say less
The same mistake happens again, in someone else's hands
columns.tip: When people are afraid, they hide mistakes, and next time the problem is caught even later.

columns.title: Blameless
items: "Why did the system let this mistake happen?"
Result: everyone speaks openly and you get the full picture
The system gets fixed: tests, guardrails, alerts
columns.tip: People will make mistakes. Build the system so that one mistake doesn't become a disaster.

blocks.code:
Title:      Checkout down for 35 minutes (SEV1), 2026-09-12
Summary:    one sentence on what happened and how many were affected

Impact:     35 minutes, ~20% of customers, 180 orders lost
Timeline:   (from the scribe's notes, minute by minute)
Root cause: (the system, not a person: "why could this happen?")
What went well: the rollback took 5 minutes
What went badly: the alert arrived 12 minutes late

Action items:
  - add an alert on payment timeouts. Owner: Rachel, by September 26
  - add a payment smoke test before deploys. Owner: Ethan, by October 3

marks.tip: Not "Ryan made a mistake" but "no test caught this before the deploy": something you can fix.
Write down what went well too; what worked needs to be kept.
Every action has one owner and a date. An action with no owner never gets done.

blocks.body: A human mistake is a signal: ask why the system let it grow into a disaster.

items: A postmortem gets written and nobody does the action list. Put the actions in tickets, track them, and check on them in the next meeting.
Writing "human error" as the root cause: that is a starting point, not a stopping point. Ask: why was it so easy to make this mistake?
Holding postmortems only for big incidents. You can learn from near-misses too.
Hold the postmortem within 2 to 3 days of the incident, while memories are fresh, and keep it open to everyone.
"Five whys": after every answer, ask "why?" again to reach the root.

check.q: Why is "Ryan ran the wrong command" the least useful line in a postmortem?
check.a: Replace Ryan and someone else can make the same mistake. The useful question: which guardrail (a test, a confirmation, a permission) would have made it impossible to run that command?
